pedagogy.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area — usually a square — and finding how many unit squares cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has an area of 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
bestPractices: Start from covering: which of several shapes covers the most surface, first by cutting/re-composing, then by covering with unit squares.
Name the unit square as '1 square unit' and area as the count of such squares that cover the region without gaps or overlaps.

Deliberately separate area from perimeter — on congruent rectangles, label the unit lengths around the edge of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the two measures are visibly different.
Establish that area is additive and unchanged under rearrangement: the same tiles cover the same area however you move them.
Use square-unit language in every answer ('12 square centimetres', not '12').
keyRepresentations: A single unit square labelled '1 square unit'
A figure on squared paper filled with unit squares, counted
Congruent rectangles: one with unit lengths marked round the perimeter, one with the interior square units drawn
The same set of tiles rearranged into different shapes (area conserved, perimeter changes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area with perimeter / length — judges the 'bigger' shape by how far it stretches or the distance around, not the surface covered.
Undifferentiated 'bigger' — calls a longer or taller shape bigger by one dimension without coordinating the 2D covering.
Thinks rearranging the same squares into a new shape changes the amount of area.
Gives area as a bare number without square units, or counts squares with gaps/overlaps.

learn.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by counting how many unit squares (the usual chosen unit of area) cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has area 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged (area is additive and conserved under recomposition). Answers should always carry square-unit language.

activities.title: Cover, count, and separate area from perimeter
feedback: If the squares leave gaps or overlap, say: area is only valid when the squares tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps — line them up edge-to-edge and count again.
If a child gives area as a bare number, prompt: 12 what? Area is counted in square units — say '12 square units' (or '12 square centimetres').

After rearranging, if a child expects the area to change, re-count the tiles together: the same 12 squares still cover 12 square units. Only the shape's outline changed, and the perimeter may or may not have changed, so count it to check.

When area and perimeter are confused, point to the filled interior (area, in square units) versus the traced edge (perimeter, in unit lengths) on the same shape so the two measures are visibly different.
activities.rationale: Building area from physically covering a region with unit squares, then separately tracing the edge, makes 'surface covered' versus 'distance around' concrete, and recomposing the same tiles exhibits conservation of area. An optional live square-unit counter and an AREA/PERIMETER toggle (interior fill vs edge trace) and a rearrange mode can make the distinction and the conservation vivid, but the same learning works with squared paper and physical square tiles.
sourceClaims: Area is the amount of two-dimensional space in a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area (often a square); a figure covered by a certain number of squares without gaps or overlaps has an area of that number of square units (3.MD.5, 3.MD.6). Area measurement assumes congruent figures enclose equal areas and that area is additive.
learnerActions: Fill a figure drawn on squared paper with unit squares, snapping them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, and count them to state the area, e.g. 'area = 12 square units'.

Trace the boundary of the SAME shape separately, stepping round the edge and counting the unit lengths, and record the perimeter in unit lengths. This is a different kind of measure from the area. For a 12-square figure the perimeter number is also different (at least 14), but for some shapes the two numbers can match: a 4-by-4 square has area 16 square units and perimeter 16 units. Even then they measure different things.
Say aloud that the squares INSIDE measure area while the steps AROUND measure perimeter — two different measures of the same shape.

Rearrange the same set of (e.g. 12) tiles, joined edge-to-edge, into a long strip. Re-count the covering squares (still 12), then re-count the perimeter and compare. For example, a 3-by-4 rectangle has perimeter 14 units, but a 1-by-12 strip has perimeter 26 units. The area count stays the same whether or not the perimeter changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares covering a region; it is distinct from perimeter and is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Label area on one rectangle, perimeter on its congruent twin
feedback: If a child treats the edge count and the interior count as the same kind of number, highlight the units: one is in square units, the other in unit lengths.
If a child insists a shape with a longer edge must have more area, set up a long-thin shape and a compact shape and count the covering squares to settle it directly.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing a perimeter-labelled rectangle with an identical area-filled rectangle addresses the common area/perimeter confusion by making each measure visible on congruent figures.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: On the first, mark the unit lengths all the way around the perimeter and total them.
On the second, draw the interior square units and count them for the area.
State in words how the two measurements differ, using square units for area and unit lengths for perimeter.
activities.intendedInsight: Area (surface covered, in square units) and perimeter (distance around, in unit lengths) are distinct attributes even of the very same rectangle.

activities.title: Predict then count: does longer mean bigger area?
feedback: If a child picks the long strip because 'it stretches further', count the squares in both: here the compact Shape A has 12 squares and the strip Shape B has 10, so A has the bigger area despite stretching less (and B even has the longer perimeter).
If a child gets the right answer but justifies it with 'it looks chunkier', push them to count the covering squares so the reason rests on the unit-square count.
For a rearrangement claim that area changed, recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-count comparison surfaces and confronts the 'longer/more spread-out is bigger' misconception, and the reasoning prompts distinguish genuine understanding from a lucky choice. Note that in the compact-12 vs strip-10 case the compact shape also has the larger area, so 'bigger area' coincides with 'more compact'; the reasoning tier plus the same-tiles rearrangement probe (same squares, area unchanged) is what truly discriminates. The chosen case does make the shape with the longer perimeter (the strip) the one with the smaller area, so area/perimeter confusion leads to the wrong pick.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at two shapes — a compact block and a long spread-out strip — and predict which has the bigger area and why.
Count the covering unit squares in each shape.
Compare your prediction with the counts and explain any difference.

Answer the follow-ups: What does the area of a shape actually tell you? If you cut a shape apart and rearrange its squares into a long line, does the area change? Why? Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area'? How is area different from the distance all the way around the edge?
activities.intendedInsight: 'Bigger area' is decided by counting covering squares, not by how far a shape stretches or how long its edge is; and area is preserved when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Sort statements: about area or about perimeter?
feedback: If a shape with a bigger perimeter is assumed to have a bigger area, revisit the long-thin-vs-compact pair where the bigger-perimeter shape has the smaller area.
Reinforce square-unit language for every area answer.
activities.rationale: Classification and comparison items are discriminating checks of the concept and its distinction from perimeter; they work as a consolidation check after hands-on covering. As a recognition-style check a sort can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction, but it does not by itself require the learner to construct and conserve area, so pair it with the covering and rearranging work.
learnerActions: Read statements and shape comparisons and sort each into 'about area' or 'about perimeter'.
For a long-thin shape and a compact shape, decide which has the bigger area and which has the bigger perimeter, and justify each by counting.
Choose, with reasons, which of several shapes has the bigger area.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can tell which questions concern surface covered (area) versus distance around (perimeter) and justify comparisons by counting.

constraints: Area answers must always be stated in square units (e.g. '12 square centimetres'), not as a bare number.
Unit squares must tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps for the count to be a valid area.

Static reference images (a labelled '1 square unit' and a 12-square figure marked 'area = 12 square units') are useful consolidation but do not let a learner rearrange tiles to experience conservation; pair them with hands-on covering and recomposition.

A sort/multiple-choice check can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction but is a recognition task; it does not by itself require independent construction or demonstrate conservation of area, so use it alongside covering and rearranging activities.
Keep the focus on 2D surface. A 3D setting risks conflating area with volume; if 3D is used, keep the measured attribute explicitly the flat surface.
The optional live counter, AREA/PERIMETER toggle, and rearrange mode are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; squared paper and physical tiles achieve the same objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original internal tension: the POE task specifies two shapes with the SAME number of unit squares (to confront conservation), while the diagnostic uses Shape A = 3×4 = 12 squares vs Shape B = 1×10 = 10 squares. The learner activity uses the diagnostic counts (where the strip also has the longer perimeter and smaller area); the reasoning tier and the same-tiles rearrangement probe (area stays 12, perimeter changes) are the stronger discriminators. Both the comparison and the conservation probe are retained.

Categorical catalog judgements that static content, dialogue, or 3D 'cannot' teach the concept are retained only as scoped limits (static images do not support rearrangement; a 3D setting risks volume confusion), not as universal claims about what a medium can teach.
Whether rearranging the 12 tiles changes the perimeter depends on the outline; it is asserted only for the specific 3×4→1×12 strip example used.
Source 'verified:true' flags and 'high' confidence are legacy metadata not re-checked in this rewrite.

assess.poeTask: Before any counting, show two shapes made from the SAME number of unit squares — one a compact block, one a long spread-out strip — and ask the child to predict which has the bigger area and WHY. Then have them count the squares in each. The equal counts confront a 'the longer/more spread-out one is bigger' prediction; the target explanation, given after counting, is that the same squares cover the same amount of surface however they are arranged.
probeDeeper: What does the area of a shape actually tell you?
If I cut Shape A apart and rearrange its 12 squares into a long line, does it still have the same area? Why?
Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area' here?
How is the area of a shape different from the distance all the way around its edge?
assess.correctAnswer: Shape A. Area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps, and A is covered by 12 squares while B is covered by 10 — so A has the bigger area, 12 square units, even though B stretches further.

errorPatterns.pattern: Area/perimeter confusion: judges 'bigger' by how far the shape stretches or the distance around its edge, so chooses the long strip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On congruent rectangles, mark the unit lengths around the perimeter of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the child sees area (surface covered) and perimeter (distance around) are different measures; then count squares to compare.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, the long strip — it stretches much further, so it covers more.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Shape B and justifies with 'it stretches further' or 'it has a longer edge/goes further round'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Undifferentiated 'bigger' by one dimension: calls the longer shape bigger from a single dimension without coordinating the two-dimensional covering.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a single object's several attributes (how long? how much surface?) to distinguish them; count the covering squares to decide area.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, because it is longer than Shape A.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Shape B 'because it is longer than A', attending only to length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation of area: believes rearranging the same squares into a different shape changes the amount of area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged; area is preserved under rearrangement (area is additive).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the rearrangement probe, says the spread-out shape has more (or less) area than the compact one made from the same squares.

responseLevels.gap: Judges 'bigger' by length, perimeter or how far the shape stretches, choosing the long strip.
responseLevels.full: Defines area as the number of unit squares covering the figure with no gaps or overlaps, compares by counting, holds it distinct from perimeter/length, and knows the area is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
responseLevels.partial: Counts unit squares to compare and gets the right answer, but the area/perimeter distinction is shaky — also thinks a longer edge means more area, or is unsure the area stays the same when the squares are rearranged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two shapes on squared paper: Shape A is a solid 3-by-4 block (12 squares) and Shape B is a long 1-by-10 strip (10 squares). Ask: 'Which shape has the bigger AREA — and how do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer alone can be guessed, so the reason tier carries it: a child who understands area counts the covering squares and picks A; a child who confuses area with length or perimeter picks the long strip B because it 'goes further'. A correct 'A' justified by 'it looks chunkier' rather than by counting squares is caught in the reason.
